local_facts.title: Ohio’s general injury deadline
local_facts.claim: Ohio Revised Code section 2305.10 generally requires a bodily-injury or product-liability action to be brought within two years after the cause of action accrues; the statute also contains different accrual rules and product-liability provisions.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The incident date, discovery facts and claim type need to be identified at the outset. A general two-year rule does not resolve every Cincinnati injury question.

local_facts.title: Shared fault and damage categories
local_facts.claim: Ohio Revised Code section 2315.33 permits recovery only when a claimant’s contributory fault is not greater than the combined tortious conduct of others, and proportionally reduces compensatory damages. Section 2315.18 separately defines economic and noneconomic loss and sets stated limits and exceptions for noneconomic damages in tort actions.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Scene evidence, witness accounts and records of economic loss can affect both liability and damages analysis; the statutory cap is not a single formula for every injury category.

local_facts.title: Hamilton County civil-case record path
local_facts.claim: The Civil Division of the Hamilton County Clerk of Courts maintains records for lawsuits including personal injury, and states that Common Pleas pleadings may be filed through e-filing.
local_facts.why_it_matters: For a Cincinnati lawsuit that belongs in Common Pleas, the local record and filing path is concrete; court and venue still require analysis of the particular claim.

anchors.label: Percentage limit on an injury contingency
anchors.detail: Ohio's fee rule forbids an illegal or clearly excessive fee and lists eight factors for judging one. It prints no percentage for a negligence claim in Cincinnati or anywhere else in the state.

anchors.label: Ceiling on noneconomic damages in a tort claim
anchors.detail: Whichever of the two is greater, and never above $350,000 for one plaintiff or $500,000 for one occurrence. Economic loss is not limited at all, and catastrophic injuries are exempt.

anchors.label: Filing a civil suit, Hamilton County Municipal Court
anchors.detail: Collected when the complaint is docketed, with service billed separately at $30 for personal or residential service and $10 for certified mail.
anchors.source_name: Hamilton County Municipal Court Civil Rule XVIII

anchors.label: Jury deposit in that same court
anchors.detail: Posted before a civil jury is seated, on top of a $10 charge for filing the jury demand itself. A motion costs $5 and a subpoena $6.
anchors.source_name: Hamilton County Municipal Court Civil Rule XVIII

fee_rows.note: Judged against eight factors: time and labor, difficulty, the charge customary in this locality, the amount involved and result, deadlines, the relationship, standing, and whether the arrangement is contingent.

fee_rows.stage: Form the contingent agreement must take
fee_rows.note: It must give the method, the separate percentages for settlement, trial and appeal, the litigation expenses being deducted, and whether they come off before or after the fee is computed.
Ohio statute requires one in every tort matter, showing how the compensation was figured, which costs and expenses were taken out, and any proposed division with referring counsel.

fee_rows.stage: Contingent fee for a criminal defendant
fee_rows.note: Ohio bars it outright, alongside contingent fees in domestic relations matters. The prohibition has nothing to do with injury work and is often confused with one.

fee_rows.stage: Workers' compensation appeal fee taxed to an employer
fee_rows.note: This dollar limit lives in the compensation appeal statute and applies when a claimant wins in common pleas. It is not a limit on a negligence contingency.

fee_rows.stage: Dollar line between the two Cincinnati courthouses
fee_rows.note: Municipal court original jurisdiction stops there, so a larger claim is filed in common pleas and draws that court's own deposit schedule instead.
